summary:
This joint resolution (S.J. Res. 186, 119th Congress, 2d Session) proposes an amendment to the United States Constitution establishing an affirmative fundamental right to vote. Introduced by Senator Durbin and nine cosigners and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, the resolution invokes the Article V amendment process, requiring a two-thirds vote in each House and ratification by the legislatures of three-fourths of the several States to become valid as part of the Constitution. The resolution does not prescribe a ratification deadline or specify a mode of ratification beyond the legislative route stated.

The proposed article contains four operative sections.

Section 1 confers an affirmative individual right: it provides that every citizen of the United States of legal voting age shall have the fundamental right to vote in any public election held in the jurisdiction of the citizen's residence. The text does not define "legal voting age," "public election," or "jurisdiction."

Section 2 establishes a substantive standard of review governing infringements of the right. It bars the United States, any State, or any political subdivision within a State from denying or abridging the fundamental right to vote unless the denial or abridgment (i) furthers a compelling governmental interest and (ii) constitutes the least restrictive means of furthering that interest. This language codifies a strict-scrutiny test as the constitutional standard applicable to voting-rights restrictions.

Section 3 effects a partial repeal of an existing constitutional provision. It repeals the phrase "or other crime" from Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment. That clause presently permits reduction of a State's basis of congressional representation when the right to vote is denied or abridged, "except for participation in rebellion, or other crime." Excising "or other crime" narrows the disenfranchisement exception preserved by that provision, leaving intact the exception for participation in rebellion.

Section 4 vests Congress with an enforcement power, authorizing legislation to enforce the article and to protect against any denial or abridgment of the fundamental right to vote. This tracks the enforcement-clause structure common to other post-Reconstruction voting amendments.

As a joint resolution proposing a constitutional amendment, the instrument carries no authorization or appropriation of funds and takes no statutory effect upon passage; its operative provisions become effective only upon ratification in accordance with Article V. The resolution amends the Constitution itself rather than any provision of the United States Code, and it contains no severability clause, effective-date provision, or savings clause.
